anchor: Let us weep at the remembrance
title: The Mu'allaqa of Imru' al-Qais in Jones's translation
greek: Arabic qifa nabki min dhikra habibin wa-manzili
short: The most famous opening in Arabic poetry, from the ode of the sixth-century prince-poet Imru' al-Qais, in Sir William Jones's prose version (1782).
body: Imru' al-Qais (sixth century; sources give his death anywhere from c. 500 to c. 565), of the royal house of Kinda in central Arabia, was regarded by later Arab critics as the greatest of the pre-Islamic poets; his Mu'allaqa heads the collection of 'suspended' odes, whose name later legend explained by the story that the poems hung on the Ka'ba. The opening words, 'Stop, let us weep at the memory of a beloved and an abode', became the most quoted line of Arabic verse. Sir William Jones (1746-94), the orientalist and jurist, translated the seven odes into English prose in 1782, numbered verse by verse, as this archive reproduces them. Jones's numbering does not always match modern Arabic editions, so these notes cite his verse numbers.

title: 'Stay!': the dual imperative
greek: Arabic qifa (dual imperative, 'stop, you two')
short: Qifa is a dual imperative, addressed to two companions; Jones's 'Stay!' cannot show the number.
body: Arabic has a dual number, and qifa means 'stop, both of you'. Ancient commentators debated whether the poet really had two companions, or whether the dual was a customary address to one companion (sometimes explained as the doubling of the imperative 'stop, stop!'); the convention of addressing two friends became standard in later poetry. Jones's 'Stay!' with its dash, then 'Let us weep', keeps the sense of a halt on a journey: the poet's party is passing the deserted camp. The companions speak in v. 3, so the scene is dramatic.

title: The ruined encampment (atlal) and the nasib
greek: Arabic atlal ('ruins'), nasib ('amatory prelude')
short: The ode begins with the poet halting at the traces of the beloved's abandoned campsite, the conventional opening (nasib) of the classical qasida.
body: The classical Arabic qasida typically opens with the nasib, the poet stopping at the faint traces (atlal) of an abandoned encampment where his beloved once lived, and remembering her; it then moves to a journey or a description of the poet's animals and exploits. Jones's 'station' renders manzil, 'place of alighting, abode'. Critics such as Jaroslav and Suzanne Stetkevych and Michael Sells read the ruined camp as an image of loss and transience in a nomadic world, and the remembered abundance of the past as its counterweight. Imru' al-Qais's poem was regarded as the model of the scene for every later poet.

title: Dahul, Haumel, Tudam and Mikra
greek: Arabic bi-siqt al-liwa bayna l-Dakhuli fa-Hawmali / fa-Tudiha fa'l-Miqrati
short: The Arabic names a chain of sites, al-Dakhul, Hawmal, Tudih and al-Miqrat, around 'the edge of the winding dune' (siqt al-liwa).
body: Jones's 'by the edge of yon bending sands' translates siqt al-liwa, the tapering end of a curving sand-dune, where the camp stood. The four names (Jones's Dahul, Haumel, Tudam and Mikra; in modern transliteration al-Dakhul, Hawmal, Tudih and al-Miqrat) are places in Najd, whose exact sites were already uncertain to medieval geographers. Naming places is itself part of the nasib's work of memory: the landscape is mapped by loss. Jones's 'Tudam' seems to reflect a reading or transcription different from the usual Tudih.

title: The winds that weave the sand
greek: Arabic lima nasajat-ha min janubin wa-sham'ali
short: The traces have not vanished because the south and north winds, blowing alternately, keep weaving sand over and off them.
body: The Arabic says the traces are not effaced 'because of what the south wind and the north have woven over them'. Ancient commentators explained that one wind covers the traces with sand and the other uncovers them, so the ruins survive. Jones's 'woven the twisted sand' keeps the textile metaphor (nasaja, 'to weave'), which suits the ripple-patterns of wind on dunes and the woven tents that once stood there. Jones places this verse inside quotation marks, making it part of the poet's speech; the Arabic has no such marks.

title: The companions' consolation
greek: Arabic la tahlik asan wa-tajammal
short: The companions halt their mounts and say, 'Do not die of grief; bear it with dignity', a formula of consolation repeated by later poets.
body: The Arabic phrase, 'Do not perish of sorrow, and bear it beautifully (tajammal)', became a stock formula; it recurs, with one word changed (tajallad, 'be steadfast'), in the second verse of Tarafa's Mu'allaqa, a sign of the shared formulaic language of pre-Islamic poetry. The poet answers that tears are his only cure, but asks what use it is to weep over an obliterated trace. The exchange makes the nasib a small drama of grief and restraint, with the virtue of patient endurance (sabr) set against the poet's indulgence in sorrow.

title: Howaira and Rebaba
greek: Arabic Umm al-Huwayrith, Umm al-Rabab, Ma'sal
short: Jones's Howaira and Rebaba are Umm al-Huwayrith and Umm al-Rabab, women the poet loved earlier, at a place called Ma'sal.
body: The Arabic names are kunyas, 'mother of al-Huwayrith' and 'mother of al-Rabab', a respectful way of naming women by a child; Jones shortened them to Howaira and Rebaba and treated them as 'damsels'. Ma'sal (Jones's Masel) is a mountain or place in Najd. The point of the verse is that the poet has suffered such partings before: love and loss repeat. Ancient commentators connected these women with stories in the poet's biography, which may have been built from the poem itself.

title: Musk and clove-gillyflowers
greek: Arabic qaranful ('clove')
short: The departing women trailed musk as the east wind (saba) carries the scent of cloves; 'clove-gillyflower' is an old English name for the clove-scented pink.
body: The Arabic compares the scent to the east wind (nasim al-saba) bringing the smell of qaranful, cloves, imported spice of the Indian Ocean trade. Jones's 'clove-gillyflowers' is the English clove pink, Dianthus caryophyllus (OED, gillyflower n.), whose name derives from Greek karyophyllon, 'clove'; so Jones substituted an English garden flower that shares the word and the scent. The east wind of morning, saba, became the classic messenger-breeze of love in Arabic and later Persian poetry, the same breeze Hafiz addresses.

title: Tears on the sword-belt
greek: Arabic mihmal ('sword-belt')
short: The poet weeps until his sword-belt is soaked: the warrior's equipment measures his grief.
body: The Arabic says the tears flowed down 'upon my throat' until they wet the mihmal, the carrier or belt of the sword. The hyperbole joins two parts of the heroic persona, the lover who weeps and the warrior who bears arms, and it is often cited as an example of Imru' al-Qais's extravagant but concrete imagery. The poet's lament now gives way to remembered pleasures: 'Yet hast thou passed many days' begins the catalogue of amorous adventures.

title: The day of Darat Juljul
greek: Arabic Darat Juljul
short: A pool where, according to a famous story, the poet surprised his cousin 'Unayza and her companions bathing and then slaughtered his camel to feed them.
body: The commentators tell that Imru' al-Qais followed the women of his tribe, among them his cousin 'Unayza, to the pool of Darat Juljul, took their clothes while they bathed, and refused to return them until each came out to fetch her own; then, to make amends, he killed his camel for them to eat, and they carried his saddle and gear home (vv. 9-10). Several scholars think the story was invented to explain the verses. Jones's 'how strange was it that they should carry his trappings' refers to this. The 'fat like the fringe of white silk' (v. 10) is one of the poem's most admired similes.

title: Onaiza's howdah
greek: Arabic khidr 'Unayzata ('the curtained litter of 'Unayza')
short: Jones's 'carriage' is the khidr, a curtained litter carried on a camel; the poet climbs into 'Unayza's, and she protests that he will lame her beast.
body: The khidr is a canopied litter (howdah) in which women travelled on camelback. 'Unayza's cry, 'Woe to thee! thou wilt compel me to travel on foot', means that his weight will exhaust her camel; the comedy is part of the poem's flirtatious realism. Jones's 'carriage' and 'vehicle' are eighteenth-century English words that turn a camel-litter into a coach. In some accounts 'Unayza is said to be his cousin, the beloved of the Darat Juljul episode.

title: Fatima
greek: Arabic afatimu mahlan ba'da hadha l-tadalluli
short: The poet addresses a Fatima, 'gently, Fatima, enough of this coquetry', in one of the most quoted love passages of the ode.
body: Jones turns 'Afatimu mahlan', 'Gently, O Fatima!', into 'away with so much coyness'. Early commentators disagreed whether Fatima is another name for 'Unayza or a different woman; the uncertainty reflects how loosely the anecdotes attach to the verses. The passage contains the famous image of her eyes as arrows that strike the broken heart (v. 20), and the request that she 'rend at once the mantle of my heart' if his manners displease her (v. 18), literally 'pull my clothes from yours', i.e. separate us.

title: The Pleiades like a jewelled sash
greek: Arabic idha ma l-thurayya fi l-sama'i ta'arradat / ta'arruda athna'i l-wishahi l-mufassali
short: The Pleiades show across the sky like the links of a jewelled sash: a famous simile marking the late hour of the night visit.
body: The Arabic compares the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), appearing obliquely in the sky, to the folds of a sash (wishah) set with jewels separated by beads. Jones's 'folds of a silken sash variously decked with gems' expands it. The time-marker belongs to the night-visit story (vv. 22-28): the poet slips past guards to the woman's tent at the hour when the Pleiades rise. Ancient critics praised Imru' al-Qais as a master of simile (tashbih), and lines like this one are why later poetry adopted the Pleiades as a jewel; compare the 'Pleiades' chain' at the end of Hafiz's ghazal in this archive.

anchor: the pure egg of an ostrich
title: Ostrich egg or pearl?
greek: Arabic ka-bikri l-muqanati l-bayadi bi-sufratin
short: The Arabic 'first-born of the white mixed with yellow' was read by commentators either as a first ostrich egg or as a pearl; Jones chose the egg.
body: The phrase bikr al-muqanat means literally the 'virgin' or first of something whose white is mixed with yellow, nourished by clear, untroubled water. Ancient commentators offered two readings: an ostrich egg, of creamy colour, a common image of a sheltered woman's complexion in early Arabic poetry; or a pearl, nourished by pure water. 'Water not yet disturbed' makes better sense of the pearl, but Jones followed the egg reading. The image praises skin protected from sun, a mark of high status.

title: The hermit's lamp
greek: Arabic manaratu mumsa rahibin mutabattili
short: Her face lights the dark like the evening lamp of a Christian monk; the image returns at v. 65 for the lightning.
body: The rahib, a Christian monk or hermit, was a familiar figure in sixth-century Arabia, living in desert cells and monasteries whose lamps were landmarks for night travellers. The Arabic speaks of 'the lamp of an ascetic monk at evening'. Imru' al-Qais uses the image twice: here for the beloved's face, and at v. 65 for the lightning, which gleams 'like the lamps of a hermit, when the oil poured on them shakes the cord'. The repetition binds the love section and the storm section of the ode, and shows the presence of Christianity in pre-Islamic Arabia.

anchor: like the billows of the ocean
title: Night like the waves of the sea
greek: Arabic wa-laylin ka-mawji l-bahri arkha sudulahu / 'alayya bi-anwa'i l-humumi li-yabtali
short: Night lets down its curtains like sea-waves to test the poet with cares; it is then pictured as a camel stretching its back and breast.
body: One of the most celebrated passages in Arabic poetry: 'many a night like the waves of the sea has let down its curtains over me with all kinds of cares, to try me.' The next verse turns night into a huge camel stretching its loins and heaving its breast, an image that Jones's 'extend her sides, to drag on her unwieldy length' renders without naming the camel. The passage marks a transition from love to endurance, and critics read it as the poet's confrontation with fate and melancholy. Jones's 'O tedious night!' and 'O hideous night!' expand the single address of the Arabic.

title: Stars tied to a rock
greek: Arabic ka-anna l-thurayya 'ulliqat fi masamiha / bi-amrasi kattanin ila summi jandali
short: The night is so long the stars seem tied with ropes to a rock; the Arabic names the Pleiades, which Jones generalises to 'the stars'.
body: In the Arabic text as usually printed, it is the Pleiades that seem fastened 'by ropes of flax to solid rocks', so that they cannot move across the sky and the night never ends. Jones generalises to 'the stars' and adds 'with strong cables'. Editions differ in the order and number of the verses in this passage, which may account for part of Jones's rendering. The hyperbole of motionless stars for an endless night of grief became a commonplace of later Arabic and Persian poetry.

title: 'The shackle of wild beasts'
greek: Arabic qaydi l-awabidi ('shackle of the wild beasts')
short: The horse is called 'the shackle of the wild game', a phrase so famous that later critics cited it as the model of a striking metaphor.
body: The Arabic verse reads: 'I go out early, while the birds are still in their nests, on a short-haired steed, the shackle of the wild beasts, huge.' Qayd al-awabid, 'the shackle of wild animals', means that the horse is so swift that the game is as good as fettered. Medieval Arab critics quoted it as one of Imru' al-Qais's inventions, often imitated by later poets. Jones explains the metaphor rather than translating it: 'so fleet as to make captive the beasts of the forest'.

anchor: a vast rock which a torrent
title: The boulder hurled by the torrent
greek: Arabic mikarrin mifarrin muqbilin mudbirin ma'an / ka-julmudi sakhrin hattahu l-saylu min 'ali
short: Four quick epithets, wheeling, fleeing, advancing, retreating 'all at once', then the horse as a boulder the flood sweeps from the heights.
body: This verse is among the most quoted in Arabic. Its first half strings four participles together, 'charging, fleeing, coming on, turning back, all at once', in a rhythm that imitates the horse's agility; the second compares the horse to a block of rock which the torrent has thrown down from above. Jones's 'Ready in turning, quick in pursuing, bold in advancing, firm in backing' tries to keep the four-beat list. The image of the flood anticipates the storm and deluge of the ode's last section.

title: Antelope, ostrich, wolf and fox
greek: Arabic lahu aytala zabyin wa-saqa na'amatin / wa-irkha'u sirhanin wa-taqribu tatfuli
short: The horse has a gazelle's flanks, an ostrich's legs, a wolf's loping trot and a young fox's gallop: a four-part animal composite.
body: The verse compares four parts or gaits of the horse to four desert animals: the flanks of a gazelle (zaby, Jones's 'antelope'), the shanks of an ostrich, the easy trot (irkha') of a wolf, and the galloping gait (taqrib) of a fox cub. Such compound comparisons were admired as precise observation by an audience that knew animals intimately. The horse section (vv. 46-63) is the longest descriptive passage of the ode and the source of countless imitations in later horse-descriptions.

title: The maidens of Duwar
greek: Arabic 'adhara Duwarin fi mula'in mudhayyali
short: The wild cows look like maidens in long trailing robes circling Duwar, a pre-Islamic idol or sacred stone around which women processed.
body: Duwar was a sacred stone or idol of pre-Islamic Arabia around which worshippers, especially young women, walked in procession, as pilgrims circled the Ka'ba. The poet compares the herd of wild cows to such maidens in long trailing cloaks (mula'). Jones's note-like phrase 'the idol Dewaar' identifies the cult object. The verse is one of the few glimpses of pre-Islamic ritual in the ode, and Suzanne Stetkevych reads the whole qasida in relation to such ritual patterns.

title: The storm and the flood
greek: Arabic a-sahi tara barqan uriki wamidahu
short: The ode closes with the poet watching distant lightning and a deluge that sweeps across named mountains of Arabia: an image of overwhelming power and renewal.
body: The last section turns from the poet's adventures to a vast rainstorm watched from afar, its lightning flickering 'like the quick glance of two hands' (Arabic ka-lam'i l-yadayni). The flood runs over a series of named places, levels palm groves and forces wild goats down from the cliffs; at daybreak the birds sing as if drunk on spiced wine (v. 74). Critics have read the storm as a counterpart to the opening ruins: the rain that once erased the camp also restores life. Some scholars, such as Sells, stress the ode's movement from loss to plenitude; others see a grand nature-piece without a single unifying design.

title: Mount Thabir and Mujaymir
greek: Arabic ka-anna Thabiran fi 'aranini wablihi / kabiru unasin fi bijadin muzammali
short: Thabir, in the downpour, looks like a tribal elder wrapped in a striped cloak; Mujaymir's summit, ringed with flood-debris, like a spindle-whorl wound with wool.
body: Thabir (Jones's Tebeir) is a mountain name in western Arabia (one Thabir overlooks Mecca). The Arabic compares it, amid the rain-clouds, to 'a great man of a people wrapped in a striped cloak (bijad)'; the next verse makes the top of al-Mujaymir (Jones's Mogaimir), surrounded by the rubbish of the flood, look like the whorl of a spindle with wool around it. Both similes domesticate the landscape: mountains become people and household objects. Medieval critics admired the precision and novelty of such comparisons, and the Iqbal Review article calls Imru' al-Qais the 'father of simile'.

title: The drowned beasts and the wild onions
greek: Arabic ka-anna l-siba'a fihi gharqa 'ashiyyatan / bi-arja'ihi l-quswa anabishu 'unsuli
short: The ode ends with beasts drowned in the flood, floating at the far edges like uprooted bulbs of wild onion (squill).
body: The last verse pictures wild animals drowned at evening, lying at the farthest edges of the flood like the uprooted roots of 'unsul, the wild onion or squill. The image is unsentimental: the storm that renews the desert also kills, and the poem ends not on human feeling but on a precise, almost comic visual likeness. Jones's 'beasts of the wood' introduces a European forest into a desert scene. That the ode closes here, without returning to the beloved, is one reason scholars long debated its unity.
